questions.title: How exactly does the partition function cancel out in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body: In Section 4, the paper substitutes the reparameterization r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x) into the Bradley–Terry model p(y_1 \succ y_2\mid x) = \sigma(r(x,y_1) - r(x,y_2)). They say the partition function term \beta \log Z(x) cancels. Can someone show the algebraic steps explicitly? I'm worried I'm missing a sign or a detail about sequence-level vs token-level rewards when showing that the \log Z(x) term cancels from the difference r(x,y_1) - r(x,y_2).

questions.title: What assumptions are needed for Theorem 1 about representing any reward class as r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that, under mild assumptions, all reward classes consistent with Plackett–Luce/Bradley–Terry can be represented via r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)} for some policy \pi. What exactly are the "mild assumptions"? Do we need \pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x) > 0 for all y (full support), or any regularity on the function class of \pi? Also, how does this depend on whether y is a full sequence vs a token, i.e., does the result implicitly require absolute continuity between \pi and \pi_\text{ref} at the sequence level?

questions.title: Why does DPO sometimes outperform PPO even with ground-truth rewards (PPO-GT)?
questions.question_body: In the sentiment control experiment, the reward–KL frontier for DPO dominates PPO and even PPO-GT (which uses the true reward). Conceptually, if both are optimizing the same KL-regularized objective, why can DPO exceed PPO with ground-truth rewards? Is the gap due to variance/baseline issues in PPO, insufficient exploration, or a mismatch in how the sequence-level KL is targeted? Any intuition on where PPO-GT loses optimality compared to maximizing the closed-form optimum implied by the DPO reparameterization?

questions.title: How is the DPO sequence-level objective computed from token-level log-probabilities?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss uses terms like \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)} for a whole completion y. In practice, are these computed as sums over tokens, i.e., \sum_t \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})}? If so, does the logistic loss \sigma(\cdot) use the total sequence-level difference between preferred and dispreferred pairs, or is there any per-token weighting? How do length effects get handled so that longer preferred sequences do not automatically dominate?

questions.title: What is the precise role of \beta in DPO compared to PPO's target KL?
questions.question_body: In Eq. (8), \beta scales the log-probability ratio inside the logistic. In PPO, one often tunes a target KL or a KL coefficient. How should I interpret \beta in DPO relative to those PPO hyperparameters? Is there an approximate mapping between a desired expected sequence-level KL and a choice of \beta, or do we need to grid search \beta per dataset and model?

questions.title: How does DPO prevent degeneration compared to a naive unlikelihood objective?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that a naive objective that increases \log \pi(y_w\mid x) and decreases \log \pi(y_l\mid x) can lead to degeneration, but DPO's gradient includes a probability weight \sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)). Can someone explain mechanistically why this weight stabilizes training? Is it essentially a hard-negative mining effect that downweights already-correct pairs and upweights misordered ones? Are there known failure modes if this weighting saturates (e.g., when \hat r_\theta is very confident but wrong)?

questions.title: Does DPO truly enforce a KL constraint, or only encourage it implicitly?
questions.question_body: The RL objective in Eq. (3) includes a KL penalty term with coefficient \beta, and the closed-form optimal policy has a log-density ratio proportional to the reward. In DPO, we optimize a logistic preference loss over log-density ratios without explicitly regularizing KL during training. Does minimizing Eq. (8) guarantee that the learned \pi_\theta will have a controlled KL to \pi_\text{ref}, or do we just hope that the learned ratios that explain preferences stay within a reasonable range? If we want a specific KL target (say, expected sequence-level KL \approx 6), how do we ensure DPO hits it?

questions.title: How sensitive is DPO to mismatch between the true data-collection policy and the chosen \pi_\text{ref}?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests initializing \pi_\text{ref} to the SFT model that generated the preference pairs, or fitting \pi_\text{ref} by MLE on preferred responses when the SFT isn’t available. If the true data-collection policy differed noticeably from the chosen \pi_\text{ref}, what bias does that induce in the DPO objective? Is there any formal robustness guarantee for off-reference data, or practical diagnostics to detect when \pi_\text{ref} is too far off?

questions.title: How does the equivalence class of rewards (differing by f(x)) interact with the KL-regularized optimal policy?
questions.question_body: Section 5 defines an equivalence relation where r and r' are equivalent if r(x,y) - r'(x,y) = f(x). Lemma 2 states that equivalent rewards induce the same optimal policy under the constrained RL problem. Could someone derive this explicitly starting from \pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\right)? It seems adding f(x) just rescales the partition function Z(x), but I want to be sure there are no edge cases (e.g., support mismatches or unnormalized densities) that break the argument.

questions.title: What is the connection between the DPO objective and a calibrated Bradley–Terry likelihood?
questions.question_body: Eq. (8) looks like fitting a Bradley–Terry model to preference data where the ‘score’ is s_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)}. Is DPO exactly MLE under a BT model over sequence-level scores s_\theta, or is there any additional regularization implied by the parameterization s_\theta = \beta(\log \pi_\theta - \log \pi_\text{ref})? Does this parameterization restrict the class of score functions compared to training an unconstrained reward head r_\phi(x,y)?

questions.title: How should we compute and report sequence-level KL in practice for DPO?
questions.question_body: The evaluation reports the average sequence-level KL \text{KL}(\pi\,\Vert\,\pi_\text{ref}), described as the sum of per-timestep KLs. In practice, for autoregressive LMs, do we estimate this as \sum_t \mathbb{E}_{y_t\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})}[\log \pi(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}) - \log \pi_\text{ref}(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})]? If so, how is the expectation approximated—by teacher forcing on sampled sequences from \pi, or on a held-out set? And does using greedy/temperature sampling affect the KL estimate, potentially confounding the reported frontiers?

questions.title: If DPO is maximizing likelihood under a preference model, where does the implicit exploration come from?
questions.question_body: PPO performs on-policy sampling during training, which provides exploration over outputs y given x. DPO, as presented, avoids sampling in the loop and uses an offline dataset of preferences. Does this mean DPO is purely offline? If the preference data is limited or biased, is there a mechanism akin to exploration to improve coverage of the output space, or must one augment DPO with additional preference data collection or self-generated pairs?

questions.title: How does DPO handle length bias or verbosity in preferences?
questions.question_body: In summarization/dialogue, longer outputs often get higher log-prob mass simply due to more tokens, and preference models can be sensitive to verbosity. Since the DPO score is the sequence-level log-ratio, does this inherently favor longer answers? The paper mentions that GPT-4 prompts were adjusted to penalize verbosity during evaluation, but what about training? Are there techniques (e.g., length normalization, per-token averaging, penalties) compatible with Eq. (8) to reduce verbosity bias without breaking the derivation?

questions.title: Is the DPO objective consistent when preference labels are noisy or non-transitive?
questions.question_body: Human preference data can be noisy and may violate transitivity. The paper mentions consistency results from generalized BT literature. Under what conditions on the data-generating process is the DPO estimator (i.e., \hat\pi_\theta that maximizes Eq. (8)) statistically consistent for the BT-style data model? Are there identifiable cases where DPO will converge to a biased solution because the Bradley–Terry assumption is violated?

questions.title: How does the normalization term in Eq. (10) relate to variance reduction in actor-critic and why is DPO more stable?
questions.question_body: Equation (10) shows an objective with f(r_\phi, \pi_\text{ref}, \beta) that includes a log-sum-exp normalization term over y. The paper says omitting it creates high variance, motivating baselines/value functions in PPO. In DPO, this term doesn’t appear explicitly. Can someone connect the dots: is DPO implicitly incorporating this normalization by working with the log-density ratio as the ‘score’? Is there a formal variance comparison that explains DPO’s empirical stability without a learned baseline?
